H1.text: A goalkeeper's high kick. A friend's flat throw. A jump over a puddle.

H2.text: Some stay in the air for ages. Some land almost at once. What decides it?

H3.text: Aarav tested it in the college corridor with a soft ball.

H4.text: He threw it at thirty degrees, then at sixty, with the same speed. Which one stays up longer?

H5.text: Most people guess, the same. Let's find the exact answer, and the reason.

P1.text: So what is the time of flight?

P2.text: It is the total time a projectile stays in the air, from leaving to landing.

P3.text: Here, it lands back at the same height it started from.

P4.text: The key idea: only the up and down motion decides when it lands. The sideways motion just comes along.

S1.text: Let's throw two balls in our motion notebook, with the same speed, twenty metres per second.

S2.text: The blue ball goes at thirty degrees. The violet ball goes at sixty degrees.

S3.text: Watch the two clocks, and the graph of height against time.

S4.text: The thirty degree ball lands first, after about two seconds.

S5.text: Slow motion at the top. The violet ball is at its top at half its flight time. Going up takes as long as coming down.

S6.text: The sixty degree ball lands after about three and a half seconds. A steeper throw has a bigger upward part, so it stays up longer.

D1.text: Now let's find the formula, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Up and down, y equals v naught sin theta times t, minus half g t squared.

D3.text: Step two. When the ball lands, it is back at height zero. So put y equals zero.

D4.text: Step three. Take t out as a common factor. t times, v naught sin theta minus half g t, equals zero.

D5.text: Step four. So either t is zero, which is the launch, or the bracket is zero.

D6.text: The bracket gives the landing time. T equals two v naught sin theta, over g.

T1.text: Remember this. Time of flight depends only on the upward part of the velocity.

C1.text: Let's check it a second way, using the top of the path.

C2.text: Going up, the upward speed falls by g every second, from v naught sin theta down to zero.

C3.text: So the time to reach the top is v naught sin theta, over g.

C4.text: Coming down takes the same time, so the total is twice that. Two v naught sin theta over g. Both ways agree.

K1.text: Side by side. At thirty degrees, sin theta is one half. T is two times twenty times a half, over nine point eight. About two seconds.

K2.text: At sixty degrees, sin theta is about zero point eight seven. T is about three point five seconds.

K3.text: Now you try. Same speed again. Which angle gives the longest time in the air? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Ninety degrees! Straight up. Sin ninety is one, the biggest sin can be. So T is two v naught over g.

B1.text: Here is a surprise. Look at what is missing from the formula.

B2.text: There is no cos theta in it. The sideways speed does not change the time at all.

B3.text: Your turn. From one table top, a ball is dropped, and another is pushed off sideways. Which lands first? Pause and think.

B4.text: Together! Both start with zero upward speed, and the same gravity. The push only makes one land farther away.

W2.text: A ball is kicked at nineteen point six metres per second, at thirty degrees. How long is it in the air?

W3.text: The upward part is v naught sin theta. Nineteen point six times one half, nine point eight metres per second.

W4.text: Time to the top is nine point eight, over nine point eight. That is one second.

W5.text: The time of flight is twice that. Two seconds.

X2.text: Many students write T equals v naught sin theta over g, and stop.

X3.text: But that is only the time to the top. The ball still has to come down. Always multiply by two.

E1.text: Where is this asked? You find the time of flight, or work back from it to the speed or the angle.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A ball is in the air for four seconds, and lands eighty metres away. g is ten. Find its launch speed and angle. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Twenty root two metres per second, at forty five degrees.

A2.text: T equals two v naught sin theta over g. So v naught sin theta is four times ten over two, which is twenty.

A3.text: Sideways, eighty metres in four seconds means v naught cos theta is twenty. Both parts are twenty, so theta is forty five degrees, and v naught is twenty root two.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why does the sideways speed not change the time of flight?

Y3.text: Two. Why is there a two in the formula?

Y4.text: Three. Which launch angle keeps a ball in the air the longest?

N1.text: Next time: the ball turns at half its flight time. But how high is that turning point? Find out in maximum height.
